answer.decision: Add jittered expirations, request coalescing, and stale-while-revalidate.
answer.action: Today, enable the cache client's single-flight primitive for the endpoint and serve stale values for up to 90 seconds while one request refreshes each key. Then deploy randomized TTL jitter so hot keys do not expire together, with TTL and stale-window settings that keep all served data within the five-minute freshness bound. Add monitoring for hit rate, coalesced requests, stale serves, refresh latency, origin query volume, and per-key load; load-test the 120 hot-key pattern before full rollout.
reasons: Duplicate origin queries for the same 120 keys caused 91 percent of the CPU spike, so per-key request coalescing directly addresses the dominant load source.
The existing single-flight primitive can be enabled immediately, making it the fastest mitigation for reducing origin load today.
Jitter prevents synchronized expiration, while stale-while-revalidate avoids a miss burst during refresh.
A 90-second stale serving window is explicitly acceptable and can be configured within the required five-minute freshness bound.
Database scaling alone improved latency but still saturated under duplicate requests; globally increasing TTL risks violating freshness requirements.
assumptions: The single-flight primitive coalesces requests by cache key across each application instance; if it is only process-local, the stale serving path and jitter still reduce cross-instance amplification.
Cache TTLs and stale-serving behavior are configurable without replacing the cache product.
The freshness age of a value can be measured or bounded so stale data is never served after five minutes.
risks: A process-local single-flight implementation may still allow one concurrent refresh per application instance.
Poorly chosen jitter or stale-window settings could exceed the five-minute freshness limit.
Refresh failures could prolong stale serving or cause a renewed origin surge when the stale window closes.
Hot-key traffic may shift, requiring monitoring beyond the currently identified 120 keys.

citations.claim: Ninety-one percent of the origin CPU spike came from repeated queries for the same 120 keys.
The cache client already provides a disabled single-flight primitive.
The endpoint must maintain freshness within five minutes.
Database scale-up did not prevent saturation under repeated duplicate requests.
Serving stale values for up to 90 seconds during refresh is acceptable if the five-minute freshness bound is preserved.
The incident included a rapid cache hit-rate collapse from 94 percent to 37 percent.
